```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>"

```

Once a study runs cleanly on your laptop via
`simulatr_check(study, B = 2)`, the next step is to scale it through
[`simulatr-pipeline`](https://github.com/Katsevich-Lab/simulatr-pipeline) —
a Nextflow workflow that benchmarks per-grid-row memory and time, shards
work across the cluster, retries on out-of-memory, and writes a
`memory.parquet` collected from the kernel's view of resident set size.

# Prerequisites

* [Nextflow](https://www.nextflow.io/) ≥ 24.04 in your `$PATH`.
* The `simulatr-pipeline` repo cloned locally (or installed via
  `nf-core download`).
* A Slurm/LSF/SGE cluster, or Docker for running locally.

The pipeline reads `inst/extdata/contract.json` from the installed
`simulatr` package and asserts at workflow start that its
`schema_version` is the one it was built against. If the assertion
fails, upgrade either the package or the pipeline so they match.

# Save the study

```{r, eval = FALSE}
saveRDS(study, "study.rds")
```

# Configure resource limits

Edit `nextflow.config` (or pass on the command line) to set the
per-grid-row resource budget. The benchmarking phase uses this to
decide how many processors to fan out per `(method, grid_row)`.

```
params {
    simulatr_specifier_fp = "study.rds"
    max_gb     = 16          // peak RAM you'll allow per task
    max_hours  = 4           // wall-clock you'll allow per task
    benchmark_memory      = 1
    benchmark_memory_base = 4
    array_size = 200         // collapse small tasks into Slurm array jobs
}
```

# Run it

On Slurm:

```
nextflow run Katsevich-Lab/simulatr-pipeline -profile slurm
```

On a laptop with Docker:

```
nextflow run Katsevich-Lab/simulatr-pipeline -profile docker,test
```

On a fresh machine, the pipeline will pull
`ghcr.io/katsevich-lab/simulatr:<version>` and use it as the worker
image, so you don't need an R install on each compute node.

# Outputs

When the workflow finishes, the result directory contains:

```
results/
├── simulatr_result.rds      # combined results + evals + summary
├── memory.parquet           # per-task memory (Layer-1 R-heap +
│                            # Layer-2 sacct/RSS)
├── errors.parquet           # one row per failed task
└── benchmarking_results.rds # Layer-1 numbers per (method, grid_row)
```

Read `memory.parquet` to find which `(method, grid_row)` is the memory
hog — see `vignette("reading-your-memory-profile")`.

# Slurm array jobs

The pipeline submits `run_simulation_chunk` and `run_benchmark` as
Slurm array jobs (set `params.array_size` to control batch width).
Instead of one Slurm job per `(method, grid_row, chunk)` — which can
mean thousands of submissions and hours of scheduler overhead — you
get one array submission per process, one task per array element.

# Errors are structured

A failed task writes `error.json` to the work directory with
`{phase, grid_id, chunk_id, run_id, type, message, traceback}`. The
`COLLECT` subworkflow concatenates these into `errors.parquet`. No
more `grep`-ing through `.command.err` files.

# Resuming

Nextflow's `-resume` flag works as expected. Each task writes a
content-addressed result file; rerunning skips tasks whose inputs are
unchanged.
